claim: EPHX1 is the first discovered epoxide hydrolase, also known as mEH.
source: The first discovered EH was EPHX1, also known as mEH.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract without supporting data in the manuscript itself, but represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: No pathogenic variants in epoxide hydrolase genes have been reported in humans prior to this study.
source: EH functions remain partly unknown, and no pathogenic variants have been reported in humans.
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge about the state of the field prior to this study.

claim: Two de novo variants in EPHX1 catalytic site were identified in patients with lipoatrophic diabetes.
source: We identified two de novo variants located in EPHX1 catalytic site in patients with a lipoatrophic diabetes characterized by loss of adipose tissue, insulin resistance, and multiple organ dysfunction.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by genetic sequencing data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The EPHX1 variants led to protein aggregation within the endoplasmic reticulum.
source: Functional analyses revealed that these variants led to the protein aggregation within the endoplasmic reticulum and to a loss of its hydrolysis activity.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The EPHX1 variants led to loss of hydrolysis activity.
source: Functional analyses revealed that these variants led to the protein aggregation within the endoplasmic reticulum and to a loss of its hydrolysis activity.
evidence: This is supported by c-SO hydrolysis assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: CRISPR-Cas9-mediated EPHX1 knockout abolished adipocyte differentiation.
source: CRISPR-Cas9-mediated EPHX1 knockout (KO) abolished adipocyte differentiation and decreased insulin response.
evidence: This is supported by Oil Red O staining and adipocyte marker expression data shown in Figure 4.

claim: CRISPR-Cas9-mediated EPHX1 knockout decreased insulin response.
source: CRISPR-Cas9-mediated EPHX1 knockout (KO) abolished adipocyte differentiation and decreased insulin response.
evidence: This is supported by insulin signaling data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: EPHX1 knockout promoted oxidative stress.
source: This KO also promoted oxidative stress and cellular senescence, an observation confirmed in patient-derived fibroblasts.
evidence: This is supported by ROS measurement data shown in Figures 5A and 6A.

claim: EPHX1 knockout promoted cellular senescence.
source: This KO also promoted oxidative stress and cellular senescence, an observation confirmed in patient-derived fibroblasts.
evidence: This is supported by SA-β-gal activity and senescence marker data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Oxidative stress and cellular senescence were confirmed in patient-derived fibroblasts.
source: This KO also promoted oxidative stress and cellular senescence, an observation confirmed in patient-derived fibroblasts.
evidence: This is supported by data from patient fibroblasts shown in Figure 6.

claim: Metreleptin therapy had a beneficial effect in one patient.
source: Metreleptin therapy had a beneficial effect in one patient.
evidence: This is supported by clinical data showing improvement in metabolic markers presented in Table 2.

claim: Five genes encoding epoxide hydrolases have been identified in humans to date.
source: The first EHs were identified more than 40 years ago, and, to date, five genes encoding EH have been identified in humans (Decker et al., 2012; Fretland and Omiecinski, 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Human microsomal and soluble EHs are also named EPHX1 and EPHX2, respectively.
source: Human microsomal and soluble EHs (mEH and sEH), also named EPHX1 and EPHX2, respectively, are the best known EHs.
evidence: This is established nomenclature in the field.

claim: Epoxide hydrolases are alpha/beta hydrolase fold enzymes.
source: Structurally, they are alpha/beta hydrolase fold enzymes.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about these enzymes.

claim: Epoxide hydrolases catalyze the rapid hydrolysis of epoxides to less-reactive and readily excretable diols.
source: They catalyze the rapid hydrolysis of epoxides, which are three membered cyclic ethers, to less-reactive and readily excretable diols (Oesch et al., 1971).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature describing the enzymatic function.

claim: In mammals, epoxides arise from cytochrome P450 oxidative metabolism of both xenobiotics and endogenous compounds.
source: In mammals, epoxides arise from cytochrome P450 (CYP450) oxidative metabolism of both xenobiotics and endogenous compounds (El-Sherbeni and El-Kadi, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Epoxides from xenobiotics are involved in the development of cancers and organ damage through interaction with DNA, lipids, and proteins.
source: Epoxides from xenobiotics are involved in the development of cancers and organ damage through interaction with DNA, lipids, and proteins (Nebert and Dalton, 2006), and EHs are necessary for their detoxification.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Epoxide hydrolases are necessary for detoxification of xenobiotic epoxides.
source: Epoxides from xenobiotics are involved in the development of cancers and organ damage through interaction with DNA, lipids, and proteins (Nebert and Dalton, 2006), and EHs are necessary for their detoxification.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Epoxy fatty acids are important regulatory lipid mediators.
source: On the other hand, epoxides derived from endogenous fatty acids, called epoxy fatty acids (EpFAs), are important regulatory lipid mediators.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of lipid signaling.

claim: Epoxy fatty acids mediate several biological processes, including inflammation, angiogenesis, vasodilation, and nociception.
source: They were shown to mediate several biological processes, including inflammation, angiogenesis, vasodilation, and nociception.
evidence: This is established knowledge about EpFA functions, though no specific citation is provided in this sentence.

claim: By regulating EpFAs levels, EHs play a key role in regulating crucial signaling pathways for cellular homeostasis.
source: By regulating EpFAs levels, EHs play a key role in regulating crucial signaling pathways for cellular homeostasis (McReynolds et al., 2020), and altered levels of EpFAs are associated with many disorders (Morisseau and Hammock, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Altered levels of EpFAs are associated with many disorders.
source: By regulating EpFAs levels, EHs play a key role in regulating crucial signaling pathways for cellular homeostasis (McReynolds et al., 2020), and altered levels of EpFAs are associated with many disorders (Morisseau and Hammock, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The full spectrum of epoxide hydrolase substrates and associated biological functions in humans remain partly unknown.
source: Although a large amount of work has been made to characterize EH functions, especially through the use of specific inhibitors and animal models, the full spectrum of their substrates and associated biological functions in human remain partly unknown (Gautheron and Jéru, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: It is a challenge to clearly define the contribution of each EH in human disorders.
source: It is also a challenge to clearly define the contribution of each EH in human disorders.
evidence: This is an inference based on the complexity of the EH system.

claim: Association studies suggested a role of several SNPs in EPHX1 and EPHX2 in multiple conditions including liver cirrhosis, alcohol dependence, Crohn's disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, preeclampsia, diabetes mellitus, and many cancers.
source: Association studies suggested a role of several single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) identified in EPHX1 [MIM132810] and EPHX2 [MIM132811] in multiple conditions, including liver cirrhosis, alcohol dependence, Crohn's disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, preeclampsia, diabetes mellitus, and many cancers (El-Sherbeni and El-Kadi, 2014; Václavíková et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The pleiotropic and crucial role of EHs in cell homeostasis is underscored by association studies.
source: This underscores the pleiotropic and crucial role of EHs in cell homeostasis, but no high-effect variants have been reported to date.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the association study data cited.

claim: No high-effect variants in epoxide hydrolase genes have been reported to date prior to this study.
source: This underscores the pleiotropic and crucial role of EHs in cell homeostasis, but no high-effect variants have been reported to date.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the field.

claim: Two unrelated patients with a complex lipoatrophic and neurodevelopmental syndrome with severe metabolic manifestations were identified carrying a de novo variant in EPHX1.
source: In the present study, we identified two unrelated patients with a complex lipoatrophic and neurodevelopmental syndrome with severe metabolic manifestations and carrying a de novo variant in EPHX1 identified by whole-exome sequencing (WES).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by genetic data.

claim: Lipoatrophic diabetes is characterized by clinical lipoatrophy due to a defect in adipose tissue storage of triglycerides.
source: Lipoatrophic diabetes, also known as lipodystrophic syndromes, are characterized by clinical lipoatrophy due to a defect in adipose tissue storage of triglycerides.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about lipodystrophic syndromes.

claim: Lipoatrophic diabetes results in ectopic lipid infiltration of non-adipose tissues leading to insulin resistance, increased liver glucose production, hypertriglyceridemia, and liver steatosis.
source: This results in ectopic lipid infiltration of non-adipose tissues leading to insulin resistance, increased liver glucose production, hypertriglyceridemia, and liver steatosis.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about the pathophysiology of lipodystrophic syndromes.

claim: About 30 genes have been implicated in lipoatrophic diabetes.
source: About 30 genes have been implicated in lipoatrophic diabetes (Brown et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Lipoatrophic diabetes remain genetically unexplained in the vast majority of cases.
source: Although these disorders remain genetically unexplained in the vast majority of cases, there is growing interest in identifying their molecular and cellular bases to improve genetic counseling and personalize treatment (Letourneau and Greeley, 2018; Sollier et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: EPHX1 is widely expressed with highest expression in the liver, adipose tissue, and adrenal glands.
source: EPHX1 is widely expressed with highest expression in the liver, adipose tissue, and adrenal glands (Coller et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: EPHX1 was the first mammalian EH to be identified and was first purified from rabbit liver in the 1970s.
source: It was the first mammalian EH to be identified and was first purified from rabbit liver in the 1970s.
evidence: This is established historical knowledge about EPHX1.

claim: EPHX1 is an evolutionarily highly conserved biotransformation enzyme.
source: It is an evolutionarily highly conserved biotransformation enzyme retained in microsomal membranes of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) (Coller et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature and conservation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: EPHX1 is retained in microsomal membranes of the endoplasmic reticulum.
source: It is an evolutionarily highly conserved biotransformation enzyme retained in microsomal membranes of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) (Coller et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: EPHX1 and EPHX2 were thought to fulfill distinct complementary roles for a long time.
source: For a long time, EPHX1 and EPHX2 were thought to simply fulfill distinct complementary roles (Decker et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: EPHX1 was well recognized to detoxify xenobiotic epoxides.
source: On the one hand, EPHX1 was well recognized to detoxify xenobiotic epoxides.
evidence: This is established knowledge about EPHX1 function.

claim: EPHX2 was shown to hydrolyze endogenous terpenoid epoxides and EpFAs.
source: On the other hand, EPHX2 was shown to hydrolyze endogenous terpenoid epoxides and EpFAs (El-Sherbeni and El-Kadi, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: EPHX1 was shown in animal models to play a significant role in the hydrolysis of different endogenous EpFAs derived from polyunsaturated fatty acids.
source: More recently, EPHX1 was also shown in animal models to play a significant role in the hydrolysis of different endogenous EpFAs derived from polyunsaturated fatty acids (Edin et al., 2018; Snider et al., 2007; Marowsky et al., 2017; Blum et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: EpFAs including EETs and EpOMEs are formed by ER-attached CYP450s and hydrolyzed by EPHX1 to their respective diols DHETs and DiHOMEs.
source: These EpFAs, including epoxyeicosatrienoic acids (EETs) and epoxyoctadecenoic acids (also called EpOMEs), are formed by ER-attached CYP450s and hydrolyzed by EPHX1 to their respective diols, the so-called dihydroxyeicosatrienoic acids (DHETs) and dihydroxyoctadecenoic acids (DiHOMEs), respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the metabolic pathway.

claim: From an evolutionary perspective, EPHX1 and EPHX2 are very different enzymes.
source: Nevertheless, from an evolutionary perspective, EPHX1 and EPHX2 are very different enzymes, which can be differentially inhibited by distinct chemical inhibitors, and display only a partially overlapping substrate selectivity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the differences between these enzymes.

claim: EPHX1 and EPHX2 can be differentially inhibited by distinct chemical inhibitors.
source: Nevertheless, from an evolutionary perspective, EPHX1 and EPHX2 are very different enzymes, which can be differentially inhibited by distinct chemical inhibitors, and display only a partially overlapping substrate selectivity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the pharmacology of these enzymes.

claim: EPHX1 and EPHX2 display only a partially overlapping substrate selectivity.
source: Nevertheless, from an evolutionary perspective, EPHX1 and EPHX2 are very different enzymes, which can be differentially inhibited by distinct chemical inhibitors, and display only a partially overlapping substrate selectivity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the substrate specificity of these enzymes.

claim: The EPHX1 variants identified in the studied patients are localized in the catalytic domain of the enzyme.
source: The EPHX1 variants identified in the studied patients are localized in the catalytic domain of the enzyme and were predicted to be pathogenic.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The EPHX1 variants identified in the studied patients were predicted to be pathogenic.
source: The EPHX1 variants identified in the studied patients are localized in the catalytic domain of the enzyme and were predicted to be pathogenic.
evidence: This is supported by in silico prediction algorithms mentioned in the Results section.

claim: Patient 1 is a 25-year-old woman originating from Mauritania.
source: The index case, patient 1, is a 25-year-old woman originating from Mauritania.
evidence: This is demographic information about the patient.

claim: Patient 1's disease phenotype was not explained by variants in genes known to be involved in lipoatrophic diabetes.
source: Her disease phenotype was not explained by variants in genes known to be involved in lipoatrophic diabetes, as assessed by the analysis of a panel of genes used in routine genetic diagnosis (Jéru et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by genetic testing data.

claim: A heterozygous variant c.997A>C, p.(Thr333Pro) in exon 7 of EPHX1 was identified in patient 1.
source: The analysis of exome data led to the identification of a heterozygous variant in exon 7 of EPHX1 (Retterer et al., 2016), which was subsequently confirmed by Sanger sequencing: c.997A>C, p.(Thr333Pro) (NM_000120.4) (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by WES and Sanger sequencing data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The variant c.997A>C, p.(Thr333Pro) was found to be de novo in patient 1 after paternity confirmation.
source: This variant was found to be de novo after paternity confirmation by genotyping a set of polymorphic markers.
evidence: This is supported by segregation analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: EPHX1 is a good candidate gene for lipoatrophic diabetes due to its key role in cellular homeostasis and fatty acid metabolism.
source: Due to the key role of EPHX1 in cellular homeostasis and fatty acid metabolism (Edin et al., 2018), this gene was a good candidate.
evidence: This is an inference based on known EPHX1 functions cited from the literature.

claim: Patient 2 is a 17-year-old woman originating from Western Europe and living in the United States.
source: Patient 2 is a 17-year-old woman originating from Western Europe and living in the United States.
evidence: This is demographic information about the patient.

claim: A de novo EPHX1 missense variant c.1288G>C, p.(Gly430Arg) located in exon 9 was identified in patient 2.
source: A second patient carrying a different de novo EPHX1 missense variant located in exon 9: c.1288G>C, p.(Gly430Arg) was identified through GeneMatcher (Sobreira et al., 2015; Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by genetic sequencing data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Patient 2 had an insulin-resistant lipoatrophic syndrome.
source: She also had an insulin-resistant lipoatrophic syndrome.
evidence: This is supported by clinical data presented in Table 1.

claim: No alternative molecular etiology compatible with the disease phenotype was identified in either of the two patients.
source: We did not identify any alternative molecular etiology compatible with the disease phenotype in either of the two patients.
evidence: This is supported by WES analysis and exclusion of other variants as detailed in Supplementary files.

claim: The EPHX1 variants were absent from databases reporting variants from the general population.
source: These variants were absent from databases reporting variants from the general population (gnomAD, ExAC, dbSNP, and Exome Variant Server), as well as from ClinVar, a database that aggregates information about genomic variations and their relationship to human diseases.
evidence: This is supported by database queries.

claim: The variants identified affect amino acids strongly conserved throughout evolution, even in zebrafish and Xenopus tropicalis.
source: The variants identified herein affected amino acids strongly conserved throughout evolution, even in zebrafish and Xenopus tropicalis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The two variants predicted changes in the polarity of the corresponding amino acids.
source: The two variants predicted changes in the polarity of the corresponding amino acids, as well as in the charge for p.Gly430Arg.
evidence: This is based on biochemical properties of the amino acid substitutions.

claim: The p.Gly430Arg variant predicted a change in charge.
source: The two variants predicted changes in the polarity of the corresponding amino acids, as well as in the charge for p.Gly430Arg.
evidence: This is based on biochemical properties of the amino acid substitution.

claim: The variants were predicted pathogenic by all tested algorithms (PolyPhen-2, SIFT, CADD).
source: They were predicted pathogenic by all tested algorithms (PolyPhen-2, SIFT, CADD).
evidence: This is supported by in silico prediction analysis.

claim: Patient 1 was born at term after a normal pregnancy without intra-uterine growth retardation.
source: This patient (woman) was born at term after a normal pregnancy without intra-uterine growth retardation.
evidence: This is clinical history data.

claim: Patient 1 had normal anthropometric parameters at birth with a height of 49 cm and a weight of 2.8 kg.
source: The anthropometric parameters at birth were normal with a height of 49 cm and a weight of 2.8 kg.
evidence: This is clinical data from birth records.

claim: Patient 1 had microcephaly with an OFC of 33 cm at birth (−1.5 SD).
source: She was first referred for dysmorphic features including microcephaly with an occipito-frontal circumference (OFC) of 33 cm at birth (−1.5 SD), which remained present in adulthood with an OFC of 51 cm (−2.5 SD) at the age of 18 years.

claim: Patient 1's microcephaly remained present in adulthood with an OFC of 51 cm (−2.5 SD) at the age of 18 years.
source: She was first referred for dysmorphic features including microcephaly with an occipito-frontal circumference (OFC) of 33 cm at birth (−1.5 SD), which remained present in adulthood with an OFC of 51 cm (−2.5 SD) at the age of 18 years.
evidence: This is clinical measurement data.

claim: Patient 1 presented with dysmorphic features including triangular-shaped face, prominent forehead, retrognathism, irregular and high hair line, high-arched palate, mandibulo-facial dysostosis, teeth misalignments, arachnodactyly, camptodactyly, joint stiffness, and clitoromegaly.
source: She also presented with a triangular-shaped face, prominent forehead, retrognathism, irregular and high hair line, high-arched palate, mandibulo-facial dysostosis including malar hypoplasia and retrognathism, teeth misalignments, arachnodactyly, camptodactyly, joint stiffness, and clitoromegaly (Figure 1C,F and Table 1).

claim: Patient 1 displayed a progressive lipodystrophic phenotype with severe lipoatrophy of the face and limbs.
source: Patient 1 also displayed a progressive lipodystrophic phenotype with severe lipoatrophy of the face and limbs (Figure 1C,G).

claim: Patient 1's lipoatrophic phenotype was confirmed by DXA with a total fat mass of 15.8%, corresponding to a Z-score of −2.8.
source: This lipoatrophic phenotype was further confirmed by dual X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) with a total fat mass of 15.8%, whereas the mean normal age-matched value is 31.4 ± 8.5% (Imboden et al., 2017), corresponding to a Z-score of −2.8.

claim: The mean normal age-matched total fat mass value is 31.4 ± 8.5%.
source: This lipoatrophic phenotype was further confirmed by dual X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) with a total fat mass of 15.8%, whereas the mean normal age-matched value is 31.4 ± 8.5% (Imboden et al., 2017), corresponding to a Z-score of −2.8.

claim: The study of segmental body composition in patient 1 revealed that the loss of adipose tissue was evenly distributed throughout the body.

claim: Patient 1's BMI was 20.2 kg/m2 at the age of 25 years.

claim: Serum leptin levels are strongly correlated with total body fat mass.
source: The serum leptin levels, which are strongly correlated with total body fat mass, were very low in patient 1 (4 ng/mL) and similar to those usually reported in partial lipodystrophy (Haque et al., 2002), further confirming the lipoatrophic phenotype.

claim: Patient 2's BMI was low (17.0 kg/m2).
source: Her BMI was low (17.0 kg/m2).
evidence: This is clinical measurement data.

claim: Patient 2 had insulin resistance, as assessed by very high fasting insulin levels (284 pmol/L), which increased over time.
source: She had insulin resistance, as assessed by very high fasting insulin levels (284 pmol/L), which increased over time.
evidence: This is laboratory measurement data.

claim: Patient 2's fasting glucose values remained in the normal range, and she was not diabetic at last investigation.
source: Her fasting glucose values remained in the normal range, and she was not diabetic at last investigation.
evidence: This is laboratory measurement data.

claim: Patient 2's serum leptin level was 3 ng/mL.

evidence: This is laboratory measurement data.

claim: Patient 2's serum adiponectin level was 0.3 mg/L.
source: Measurement of serum levels of leptin (3 ng/mL) and adiponectin (0.3 mg/L) further confirmed the lipoatrophic and insulin-resistant phenotype.
evidence: This is laboratory measurement data.

claim: Patient 2 had severe hypertriglyceridemia (21.9 mmol/L) associated with low HDL-cholesterol levels (0.52 mmol/L).
source: She had severe hypertriglyceridemia (21.9 mmol/L) associated with low HDL-cholesterol levels (0.52 mmol/L).
evidence: This is laboratory measurement data.

claim: Patient 2's liver enzymes were elevated: AST (71 IU/L), ALT (94 IU/L), and ALP (145 IU/L).
source: Liver enzymes were elevated: AST (71 IU/L), ALT (94 IU/L), and ALP (145 IU/L).
evidence: This is laboratory measurement data.

claim: Patient 2's liver ultrasound demonstrated fatty infiltrate.

claim: Patient 2 had profound sensorineural hearing loss since birth requiring cochlear implants.
source: She also had profound sensorineural hearing loss since birth requiring cochlear implants.
evidence: This is clinical assessment data.

claim: Patient 2's brain CT and EEG were normal.
source: Brain computerized tomography and electroencephalogram were normal.
evidence: This is imaging and electrophysiological data.

claim: Patient 2's parents were clinically unaffected.
source: The parents of patient 2 were clinically unaffected.
evidence: This is clinical examination data of family members.

claim: The two affected individuals share a number of clinical features including dysmorphic features, lipoatrophy, insulin resistance, hypertriglyceridemia, liver dysfunction, and bilateral sensorineural hearing loss.
source: Altogether, these data demonstrate that the two affected individuals have a complex disease phenotype and share a number of clinical features including dysmorphic features, lipoatrophy, insulin resistance, hypertriglyceridemia, liver dysfunction, and bilateral sensorineural hearing loss.
evidence: This is a summary of clinical data from both patients.

claim: EPHX1 encodes a protein of 455 residues.
source: EPHX1 encodes a protein of 455 residues.
evidence: This is established structural information about the protein.

claim: EPHX1 is retained in microsomal membranes of the ER by a single transmembrane segment located at the N-terminus comprising around 20 amino acids.
source: The enzyme is retained in microsomal membranes of the ER by a single transmembrane segment located at the N-terminus and comprising around 20 amino acids (Friedberg et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The C-terminal part of EPHX1 is exposed at the cytosolic membrane surface and constitutes the catalytic domain.
source: The C-terminal part of the protein, containing the two variants identified, is exposed at the cytosolic membrane surface and constitutes the catalytic domain (Lewis et al., 2005; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: The EPHX1 mechanism of hydrolysis involves two chemical steps: a fast-nucleophilic attack leading to formation of an ester intermediate, followed by hydrolysis mediated by a water molecule activated by a charge relay system.
source: The EPHX1 mechanism of hydrolysis involves two chemical steps. A fast-nucleophilic attack leads to the formation of an ester intermediate, a covalent bond linking the substrate to the enzyme. Thereafter, hydrolysis of this complex to the final diol product is mediated by a molecule of water activated by a charge relay system (Oesch et al., 2000; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: The EPHX1 active site is composed of a catalytic triad consisting of Asp226, Glu404, and His431.
source: The EPHX1 active site is composed of a so-called catalytic triad consisting of Asp226, Glu404, and His431.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about the enzyme.

claim: Two tyrosine residues (Tyr299 and Tyr374) provide essential support to EPHX1 catalysis by polarizing the epoxide.
source: In addition, two tyrosine residues (Tyr299 and Tyr374) provide an essential support by polarizing the epoxide (Oesch et al., 2000; Bell and Kasper, 1993; Arand et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The localization of the mutated amino acids within the 3D protein structure strongly supported their pathogenic effect.
source: The localization of the mutated amino acids within the three-dimensional (3D) protein structure strongly supported their pathogenic effect.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The exact structure of EPHX1 is still not available.
source: Although the exact structure of EPHX1 is still not available, the quaternary structure of a closely homologous enzyme was determined from the fungus Aspergillus niger (Zou et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated as current knowledge about available structural data.

claim: The quaternary structure of a closely homologous enzyme to EPHX1 was determined from the fungus Aspergillus niger.
source: Although the exact structure of EPHX1 is still not available, the quaternary structure of a closely homologous enzyme was determined from the fungus Aspergillus niger (Zou et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Glycine 430 is located beside His431, which is directly implicated in the water activation and hydrolytic step of the catalytic process.
source: Glycine 430 mutated in patient 2 is located beside the crucial His431, which is directly implicated in the water activation and hydrolytic step of the catalytic process (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A 3D structure model from the SWISS-MODEL repository was used to determine the location of Thr333.
source: We used a 3D structure model from the SWISS-MODEL repository to determine the location of Thr333 (Waterhouse et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the structural modeling approach.

claim: On the 3D structure, Thr333 appears in close vicinity to Gly430 and to the three critical residues of the catalytic site (Asp226, Glu404, His431).
source: On the 3D structure, this residue appears in close vicinity to Gly430, as well as to the three critical residues of the catalytic site (Asp226, Glu404, His431) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The location of the two de novo EPHX1 variants suggests that they could affect the enzyme activity.
source: The location of the two de novo EPHX1 variants suggests that they could affect the enzyme activity and argues for their pathogenic effect.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis.

claim: Overexpression of hEPHX1WT in HEK 293 cells led to high c-SO hydrolysis, as compared to untransfected cells in which it was undetectable.
source: c-SO hydrolysis in lysates of HEK 293 cells overexpressing hEPHX1WT was high, as compared to untransfected cells in which it was undetectable.
evidence: This is supported by enzyme activity assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The p.Thr333Pro and p.Gly430Arg variants led to a near-complete absence of EPHX1 enzyme activity.
source: The two variants identified in patients, p.Thr333Pro and p.Gly430Arg, led to a near-complete absence of this enzyme activity (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This is supported by enzyme activity assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Neither overexpression of hEPHX1Tyr113His nor that of hEPHX1His139Arg led to reduced c-SO hydrolysis in HEK 293 lysates as compared to hEPHX1WT.
source: Neither overexpression of hEPHX1Tyr113His nor that of hEPHX1His139Arg led to reduced c-SO hydrolysis in HEK 293 lysates as compared to hEPHX1WT (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This is supported by enzyme activity assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The p.Glu404Asp variant did not significantly modify the hydrolysis of c-SO compared to hEPHX1WT.
source: This variant did not significantly modify the hydrolysis of c-SO compared to hEPHX1WT (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This is supported by enzyme activity assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The protein expression level was slightly diminished for the p.Gly430Arg variant.
source: Although the protein expression level was slightly diminished for the p.Gly430Arg variant, there was no significant difference in the expression of the WT and other mutated isoforms (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: There was no significant difference in the expression of the WT and other mutated EPHX1 isoforms (except p.Gly430Arg).
source: Although the protein expression level was slightly diminished for the p.Gly430Arg variant, there was no significant difference in the expression of the WT and other mutated isoforms (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The p.Thr333Pro and p.Gly430Arg variants strongly impair EPHX1 hydrolysis function by altering its catalytic triad domain.
source: Collectively, these data showed that the p.Thr333Pro and p.Gly430Arg variants strongly impair EPHX1 hydrolysis function by altering its catalytic triad domain (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from enzyme activity and structural data.

claim: An accumulation of 7,8 epoxydocosapentaenoic acid and a decrease of the corresponding diol (7,8 dihydroxydocosapentaenoic acid) was observed in patient 1's plasma.
source: An accumulation of 7,8 epoxydocosapentaenoic acid, and a decrease of the corresponding diol (7,8 dihydroxydocosapentaenoic acid), was observed (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: mEH plays a significant role in the metabolism of 7,8 epoxydocosapentaenoic acid.
source: A recent study shows that mEH plays a significant role in the metabolism of this EpFA (Morisseau et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent literature.

claim: EPHX1 is mainly localized in the microsomal fraction of the ER.
source: As mentioned previously, EPHX1 is mainly localized in the microsomal fraction of the ER (Coller et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Co-staining with calnexin confirmed that hEPHX1WT is located in the ER, as well as all mutated EPHX1 isoforms.
source: Co-staining with calnexin, which is a marker of ER, confirmed that hEPHX1WT is located in the ER, as well as all mutated EPHX1 isoforms carrying the five previously mentioned missense variants (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The EPHX1 isoforms carrying the p.Thr333Pro and p.Gly430Arg variants formed higher-order complexes or clumps within the ER, as compared to WT hEPHX1 and other mutated isoforms.
source: However, the EPHX1 isoforms carrying the two de novo variants identified in patients (p.Thr333Pro and p.Gly430Arg) were also found to form higher-order complexes or clumps within the ER, as compared to WT hEPHX1 and other mutated isoforms (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The two de novo variants still led to EPHX1 aggregation within the ER when the Flag tag was removed.
source: Of note, the two de novo variants still led to EPHX1 aggregation within the ER when the Flag tag was removed (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Both hEPHX1Thr333Pro and hEPHX1Gly430Asp proteins were revealed as two bands by western blot: one corresponding to the protein monomer around 55 kDa, and another to an oligomer around 150 kDa.
source: The presence of these oligomers was further confirmed by western blot analysis since both hEPHX1Thr333Pro and hEPHX1Gly430Asp proteins were revealed as two bands, one corresponding to the protein monomer around 55 kDa, and another to an oligomer around 150 kDa (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: When cell lysates were enriched in EPHX1 by immunoprecipitation, western blot analysis revealed an increase of higher-order complexes in the presence of the p.Thr333Pro and p.Gly430Arg variants.
source: When the cell lysates were enriched in EPHX1 by immunoprecipitation with an anti-Flag antibody, western blot analysis using an anti-hEPHX1 antibody revealed an increase of these higher-order complexes in the presence of the two p.Thr333Pro and p.Gly430Arg variants (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The p.Thr333Pro and p.Gly430Arg variants confer an aberrant conformation to EPHX1 leading to its aggregation.
source: All these data demonstrate that the p.Thr333Pro and p.Gly430Arg variants confer an aberrant conformation to EPHX1 leading to its aggregation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from immunofluorescence and western blot data.

claim: EPHX1 aggregation likely contributes to abolish the enzyme catalytic activity through a dominant negative mechanism.
source: This likely contributes to abolish the enzyme catalytic activity through a dominant negative mechanism.
evidence: This is speculation based on the aggregation data.

claim: A major loss of Ephx1 expression was observed in 3T3-L1 KO cells, which remained stable over time during adipocyte differentiation.
source: KO efficiency was further confirmed by western blot analysis. A major loss of Ephx1 expression, which remained stable over time during adipocyte differentiation, was indeed observed (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Hydrolysis of [3H]-cSO revealed a significant loss of enzyme activity in 3T3-L1 KO cells, as compared to control cells.
source: Consistently, hydrolysis of [3H]-cSO was evaluated in cell lysates and revealed a significant loss of enzyme activity in 3T3-L1 KO cells, as compared to control cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by enzyme activity assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: WT and control 3T3-L1 pre-adipocytes differentiated into adipocytes within 12 days and displayed strong accumulation of lipid droplets in the cytoplasm.
source: WT and control 3T3-L1 pre-adipocytes differentiated into adipocytes within 12 days and displayed strong accumulation of lipid droplets in the cytoplasm (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is supported by Oil Red O staining data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Ephx1 KO led to strong and significant decrease in lipid droplet formation (p< 0.0001).
source: In contrast, Ephx1 KO led to strong and significant decrease in lipid droplet formation (p< 0.0001) (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is supported by Oil Red O staining data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Ephx1 KO cells displayed a significantly reduced expression of adipogenic markers, including PPARγ, C/EBPα, SREBP-1c, as well as reduced expression of mature adipocyte markers, such as FAS and adiponectin.
source: As compared to WT and control cells submitted to in vitro adipocyte differentiation, Ephx1 KO cells displayed a significantly reduced expression of adipogenic markers, including peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARγ), CCAAT/enhancer-binding protein alpha (C/EBPα), SREBP-1c, as well as reduced expression of mature adipocyte markers, such as fatty acid synthase (FAS), and adiponectin (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: In WT and control 3T3-L1 adipocytes stimulated with insulin, western blot analysis revealed a strong increase in the phosphorylation of IRβ, IRS1, AKT, and ERK.
source: In WT and control 3T3-L1 adipocytes stimulated with insulin, western blot analysis revealed a strong increase in the phosphorylation of several signaling intermediates from the mitotic and metabolic pathways including insulin receptor β subunit (IRβ), insulin receptor substrate-1 (IRS1), AKT, and extracellular-regulated kinase (ERK) (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The Ephx1 KO cells were resistant to insulin, both in pre-adipocytes and in differentiated cells, as shown by the lack or strong decrease in the phosphorylation of IRβ, IRS1, AKT, and ERK upon insulin stimulation.
source: In contrast, the Ephx1 KO cells were resistant to insulin, both in pre-adipocytes and in differentiated cells, as shown by the lack or strong decrease in the phosphorylation of these intermediates upon insulin stimulation (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: A new KO cellular model using another gRNA targeting Ephx1 exon 5 had a similar defect in adipocyte differentiation as the first KO cell line.
source: As revealed by Oil Red O staining, this new KO cellular model had a similar defect in adipocyte differentiation as the first KO cell line used throughout this study (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by Oil Red O staining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: Ephx1 deficiency alters adipogenesis and inhibits insulin signaling, consistent with the lipoatrophic and insulin-resistant phenotype.
source: Taken together, these results show that Ephx1 deficiency alters adipogenesis and inhibits insulin signaling, consistent with the lipoatrophic and insulin-resistant phenotype.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the adipocyte differentiation and insulin signaling data.

claim: A previous study has shown that EPHX1 might protect cells from oxidative stress.
source: A previous study has shown that EPHX1 might protect cells from oxidative stress (Cheong et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Increased cellular senescence has been functionally linked to fat-related metabolic dysfunction.
source: In addition, increased cellular senescence has been functionally linked to fat-related metabolic dysfunction (Tchkonia et al., 2010) and has been observed in a few lipodystrophic syndromes (Bidault et al., 2013; Fiorillo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Increased cellular senescence has been observed in a few lipodystrophic syndromes.
source: In addition, increased cellular senescence has been functionally linked to fat-related metabolic dysfunction (Tchkonia et al., 2010) and has been observed in a few lipodystrophic syndromes (Bidault et al., 2013; Fiorillo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cellular aging has been associated with an increased production of reactive oxygen species.
source: Cellular aging has also been associated with an increased production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Davalli et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Ephx1 KO cells displayed higher levels of ROS in cell lysates, compared to either WT or control 3T3-L1 cells (p<0.0001).
source: Ephx1 KO cells displayed higher levels of ROS in cell lysates, compared to either WT or control 3T3-L1 cells (p<0.0001) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by ROS measurement data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: BrdU incorporation was lower in Ephx1 KO cells compared to WT and control cells (p<0.0001), consistent with a reduced proliferation rate.
source: Bromodeoxyuridine (BrdU) incorporation was lower in Ephx1 KO cells compared to WT and control cells (p<0.0001), consistent with a reduced proliferation rate (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by BrdU incorporation assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The levels of P21 and P16 were significantly increased in Ephx1 KO cells, consistent with increased senescence.
source: In parallel, the levels of P21 and P16, two cell cycle cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors were significantly increased in KO cells, consistent with increased senescence (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Ephx1 KO cells were characterized by a significant increase in SA-β-gal activity (p<0.0001), which is a marker of cellular senescence.
source: Additionally, compared to WT and control 3T3-L1 cells, Ephx1 KO cells were characterized by a significant increase in senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-gal) activity (p<0.0001), which is another marker of cellular senescence (Figure 5D,E; López-Otín et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by SA-β-gal staining data shown in Figure 5D,E.

claim: Enhanced levels of phosphorylated P53 were observed in Ephx1 KO cells, further underlining the senescent cellular phenotype.
source: Finally, enhanced levels of phosphorylated P53 were observed in KO cells (Figure 5C), further underlining the senescent cellular phenotype (Qian and Chen, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: EPHX1 KO in human ASCs led to a major increase in cellular senescence, as assessed by the significant increase in SA-β-gal activity (p<0.001) and enhanced levels of phosphorylated P53, P21, and P16.
source: This KO led to a major increase in cellular senescence, as assessed by the significant increase in SA-β-gal activity (p<0.001) (Figure 5G,H) and enhanced levels of phosphorylated P53, P21, and P16 (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by SA-β-gal staining and western blot data shown in Figure 5F,G,H.

claim: The level of senescence in EPHX1 KO ASCs was so high (~20-fold increase) that it prevented the cells from being further differentiated into adipocytes.
source: The level of senescence was so high (~20-fold increase) that it prevented the EPHX1 KO ASCs to be further differentiated into adipocytes.
evidence: This is an observation from the ASC differentiation experiments.

claim: Data obtained in a murine cell line and validated in a human cellular model strongly argue for a functional link between EPHX1 dysfunction, oxidative stress, and cellular senescence.
source: Altogether, these data obtained in a murine cell line and validated in a human cellular model strongly argue for a functional link between EPHX1 dysfunction, oxidative stress, and cellular senescence.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ROS and senescence data in both 3T3-L1 and ASC models.

claim: EPHX1 protein was detected by western blot in cultured fibroblasts from skin biopsies of two normal individuals (T1 and T2) and patient 1.
source: Although skin is not a tissue in which EPHX1 is highly expressed, the protein was detected by western blot in cultured fibroblasts from skin biopsies of two normal individuals (T1 and T2) and patient 1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Immunoblot analyses using several anti-EPHX1 polyclonal antibodies allowed detection of only the monomeric EPHX1 form (55 kDa) but not the higher-order complexes in fibroblasts.
source: These immunoblot analyses using several anti-EPHX1 polyclonal antibodies allowed us to detect only the monomeric EPHX1 form (55 kDa) but not the higher-order complexes.
evidence: This is an observation from western blot experiments on fibroblasts.

claim: The mutant fibroblasts from patient 1 showed increased levels of ROS in cell lysates compared with controls (p<0.0001).
source: The mutant fibroblasts showed increased levels of ROS in cell lysates compared with controls (p<0.0001) (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by ROS measurement data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Patient 1-derived fibroblasts displayed an altered morphology with an enlarged, flattened, and irregular shape, as compared to spindle-shaped control fibroblasts.
source: Regarding the impact of the EPHX1 variant on cellular senescence, the patient 1-derived fibroblasts displayed an altered morphology with an enlarged, flattened, and irregular shape, as compared to spindle-shaped control fibroblasts (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: BrdU incorporation was significantly reduced in patient 1-derived mutant fibroblasts (p<0.0001), which was correlated with increased levels of P21 and P16.
source: BrdU incorporation was significantly reduced in mutant fibroblasts (p<0.0001), which was correlated with increased levels of P21 and P16 (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is supported by BrdU incorporation and western blot data shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: SA-β-gal activity was markedly increased in patient 1-derived mutant fibroblasts (p<0.0001), even though these fibroblasts were at an earlier passage than controls.
source: Furthermore, SA-β-gal activity was markedly increased in the mutant fibroblasts (p<0.0001), even though these fibroblasts were at an earlier passage than controls (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This is supported by SA-β-gal staining data shown in Figure 6D,E.

claim: Increased SA-β-gal activity in patient 1-derived fibroblasts was accompanied by enhanced levels of phosphorylated P53.
source: This increased SA-β-gal activity was accompanied by enhanced levels of phosphorylated P53 in mutant fibroblasts (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Results from patient 1-derived fibroblasts were similar to those obtained using Ephx1-KO pre-adipocytes, confirming ex vivo the key role of EPHX1 in controlling senescence-associated oxidative stress.
source: Together, these results were similar to those obtained using Ephx1-KO pre-adipocytes, confirming ex vivo the key role of EPHX1 in controlling senescence-associated oxidative stress.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing fibroblast and 3T3-L1 data.

claim: The gnomAD database reports several dozen predicted loss-of-function variants in EPHX1, including nonsense, frameshift, and canonical splice site variants.
source: The gnomAD database, which collects variants from the general population, reports several dozen predicted loss-of-function variants in EPHX1, including nonsense, frameshift, and canonical splice site variants.
evidence: This is information from the gnomAD database.

claim: The pathogenic effect of the missense variants identified in patients 1 and 2 may be associated with a dominant negative mechanism, not only due to a loss-of-function.
source: This suggests that the pathogenic effect of the missense variants identified in patients 1 and 2 is not only due to a loss-of-function, but may be associated with a dominant negative mechanism.
evidence: This is speculation based on the presence of loss-of-function variants in the general population.

claim: A previous study on the 3D-structure of EPHX1 suggests that this enzyme might be dimeric.
source: A previous study on the 3D-structure of EPHX1 suggests that this enzyme, which is mostly membrane bound, might be dimeric (Zou et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: A dimeric structure of EPHX1 would be in favor of a dominant negative effect.
source: This would be in favor of a dominant negative effect, as well as the formation of higher-order complexes within the ER observed in overexpression studies.
evidence: This is speculation based on structural considerations.

claim: No dominant negative effect was detected in the c-SO hydrolysis assay when co-expressing WT and mutated forms of EPHX1.
source: We did not detect any dominant negative effect in the c-SO hydrolysis assay when co-expressing WT and mutated forms of EPHX1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by enzyme activity assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Overexpression studies are probably not the most appropriate system to investigate dominant negative properties of EPHX1 variants.
source: However, overexpression studies are probably not the most appropriate system to investigate such properties.
evidence: This is a methodological consideration.

claim: The final result of the EPHX1 variants is a loss of the enzyme activity, consistent with the localization of the variants at the center of EPHX1 catalytic site.
source: In any case, the final result is a loss of the enzyme activity, consistent with the localization of the variants at the center of EPHX1 catalytic site.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from enzyme activity and structural data.

claim: EPHX1 KO in 3T3-L1-pre-adipocytes revealed a high rate of ROS production, an observation confirmed in patient 1-derived fibroblasts.
source: EPHX1 KO in 3T3-L1-pre-adipocytes revealed a high rate of ROS production, an observation confirmed in patient 1-derived fibroblasts.
evidence: This is a summary of ROS data from both cell types.

claim: These data reinforce the proposed role of EHs as regulators of oxidative stress.
source: These data reinforce the proposed role of EHs as regulators of oxidative stress (Cheong et al., 2009; Inceoglu et al., 2017; Ulu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Patient 1-derived fibroblasts displayed an altered morphology, senescent features such as an increase in the SA-β-gal marker, as well as a reduced proliferative rate.
source: Patient 1-derived fibroblasts displayed an altered morphology, senescent features such as an increase in the SA-β-gal marker, as well as a reduced proliferative rate.
evidence: This is a summary of senescence data from patient fibroblasts.

claim: The senescent phenotype observed in patient fibroblasts was reproduced by removing EPHX1 in 3T3-L1 pre-adipocytes and ASCs, which subsequently lost their capacity to differentiate into adipocytes.
source: This senescent phenotype was reproduced by removing EPHX1 in 3T3-L1 pre-adipocytes and ASCs, which subsequently loss their capacity to differentiate into adipocytes.
evidence: This is a summary of senescence and differentiation data from multiple cell types.

claim: The findings support the notion that cellular senescence is an important player in adipogenesis.
source: Our findings not only support the notion that cellular senescence is an important player in adipogenesis, but also argue that EPHX1 might directly regulate adipocyte differentiation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the senescence and adipogenesis data.

claim: EPHX1 might directly regulate adipocyte differentiation.
source: Our findings not only support the notion that cellular senescence is an important player in adipogenesis, but also argue that EPHX1 might directly regulate adipocyte differentiation.
evidence: This is speculation based on the adipogenesis data.

claim: Ephx1 knockout mice have already been generated.
source: Regarding available animal models, Ephx1 knockout mice have already been generated (Miyata et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Deletion of Ephx1 in the heterozygous or homozygous state did not induce an obvious phenotype in mice, and histological examination of several organs revealed no difference between Ephx1-null mice and wild-type littermates.
source: Deletion of the gene in the heterozygous or homozygous state did not induce an obvious phenotype and histological examination of several organs revealed no difference between Ephx1-null mice and wild-type littermates.
evidence: This is information from the cited mouse study.

claim: There are differences between human and murine fat distribution and lipid metabolism, particularly the handling and oxidation of lipids.
source: The first complexity when attempting to model lipodystrophy in mice is the differences between human and murine fat distribution and lipid metabolism, particularly the handling and oxidation of lipids (Rochford, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Observations made in models of congenital generalized lipodystrophies can translate quite accurately from mice to humans.
source: So far, it appears that observations made in models of congenital generalized lipodystrophies (CGL) can translate quite accurately from mice to humans.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CGL mouse models.

claim: The most frequent CGL are autosomal recessive disorders due to bi-allelic null variants.
source: Indeed, the most frequent CGL are autosomal recessive disorders due to bi-allelic null variants.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CGL genetics.

claim: Familial partial lipodystrophy syndromes are more difficult to study in mice, since they are often autosomal dominant and some variants induce a dominant negative effect.
source: In contrast, familial partial lipodystrophy syndromes are more difficult to study in mice, since they are often autosomal dominant and some variants induce a dominant negative effect (Garg, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Knock-in mice would be required to better investigate pathophysiological mechanisms for EPHX1 variants.
source: Knock-in mice would be required to better investigate such pathophysiological mechanisms for EPHX1 variants, and additional metabolic stress is sometimes needed to uncover more aspects of the human phenotype (Gray et al., 2006).
